newsitem.title: CHILE: COPPER - Small Chilean copper mines face crisis.
newsitem.headline: COPPER - Small Chilean copper mines face crisis.

text.p: Hundreds of small and medium sized Chilean copper mines are facing ruin as the result of tumbling world copper prices and the lack of investment in the sector, said the National Mining Society (Sonami).

"Many small mines are disappearing and being forced out of business by the fall in copper prices and the lack of up-to-date technology," said Patricio Cespedes, vice-president of Sonami, which represents most of Chile's private mining companies.

Figures from Sonami paint a gloomy picture of a rash of closures with the number of small producers falling to 500 last year from 1,300 in 1993 and output dropping from 32,000 tonnes three years ago to around 21,000 tonnes in 1996.
The slide in prices this year will force even more to the wall as their operating costs, which average over a dollar a pound, are above current copper prices, said Cespedes.
Although the pits employ less than 4,000 people, they are the mainstay of many small mining communities scattered in the desolate northern Atacama Desert and in more heavily populated central Chile.
"There is a lack of interest in the sector," he said.
"If they could use up-to-date technology, then costs could fall to $0.80 cents a pound," he said.

Enami should invest in small-scale plants to allow mineral from these pits to be processed using the solvent extraction-electro-winning method which is cheaper and cleaner than more tradtional methods, said Cespedes.
The pits are also burdened by debts of over $2 million to Enami for loans made to miners in recent years, he said.

Enami officials say the company raised subsidies recently to small and medium-sized producers to $14 a tonne for copper concentrates and is continuing to invest in exploration projects which will benefit the pits.
"The small and medium-sized mining sector has always been in crisis -- if not for one reason, then for another," said Ivan Enriquez, a mining consultant with Enami.
"Enami is doing all that it can to improve the situation."
Their situation is in stark contrast to the country's huge industrial mining sector -- where many pits are over 100,000 tonnes and whose costs are among the world's lowest.
The recently-opened El Abra pit can mine copper for $0.35 a pound cash cost and even state-owned giant Codelco, which has long battled high costs, can churn out the metal for $0.48.

The crisis is the result of the failure by state mining company Enami, which has responsibility for the small and medium sized mining projects, to invest in exploration and modern low-cost technology, said Cespedes.
